Most people will ask "Why?", and you're going to need to produce a
reason for it. If the reason for the action will help you gain the
most VPs possible out of the current game, then go for it. Plausible
in-game reasons could include "I have an Amaranth, he's the only older
vampire, and I want a free skill card", "He's a voter and my
bruise-and-vote deck wants vote lock", or the like. You won't make
the guy across the table HAPPY, but at least these actions have a
direct benefit to your deck and are related to the current game,
however flimsily.

If the reason for the action isn't going to help you gain VPs, expect
to catch some grief over it. If it's not based on in-game
considerations ("he broke a deal with me last game" is NOT in-game),
expect to be warned or penalized appropriately.

>Even though last game the guy cross table(that I am attacking) broke
>an agreement with me, and whines that I am picking on him for "out of
>game" reasons.

Well, are you, or not?

>Because I, for one, will not go around inventing reasons to defend
>what I want to do in a game that is based on subjective stragetys.
>If, in my mind, I want to attack the guy across table it's up to me.

And it'll be up to the judge to determine whether or not you're trying
to play V:TES, or whether you're trying to play "screw the guy across
the table". The first is what you signed up to the tournament for.
The second, you can play on your own time, since 4 other people are
sitting at the table with you who are (theoretically) trying to play
V:TES.

>I shouldn't have to explain that..."Uhm..my deck always loses to
>malkavian sneak bleed decks...but...uh...since my prey has a
>ravnos...and...I think that maybe he's got a sneak bleed deck...even
>though he did lie and bleed me out last game...uhm..I feal that for
>victory points in this game I should kill him..yeah thats it."

You're perfectly welcome to try to make such an explanation. If it's
crap, it'll be obviously crap and can be discarded appropriately.

>Is it judges or other players that will 'decide' what is collusion and
>what I can and can't do with my own deck? Or is this just a rule made
>up to pick on certain players that noone likes, or that admit to using
>pre-determined tactics to cheat? (cause it seems totally pointless)

Judges should be the only ones doing the deciding. Other players will
be doing the yelling and bitching, but the JUDGE'S decision is the
only one that matters.

This rule was created (IMO) because players have been admitting to
sacrificing their own VPs in preliminary rounds in a deliberate
attempt to keep decks that can stop theirs out of the final round.
This isn't playing V:TES, it's just screwing around with the
tournament itself.

Depends on context (see below). If you've never played a game with that
player before at this tournament, you're either (a) being a random
goofyhead or (b) for some reason that vampire really hoses your deck
and you need it gone -- fast.

(a) gets you an untracked verbal caution. (b) probably gets you off
the hook.

>Even though last game the guy cross table(that I am attacking) broke
>an agreement with me, and whines that I am picking on him for "out of
>game" reasons.

If there's really good evidence (such as a broken deal last game) that
you're just doing it out of spite, and your justifications are particularly
flimsy, you're definitely getting a tracked warning. I knows spite
when I sees it. This sort of thing is always up to the judge -- there's
no way to hard-and-fast define spite, because spiteful people will always
go right up as far as they can to the prohibited line wherever you draw it.

>Because I, for one, will not go around inventing reasons to defend

>what I want to do in a game that is based on subjective stragetys. (sic)

No need to invent reasons; just use valid ones.

>If, in my mind, I want to attack the guy across table it's up to me.
>I shouldn't have to explain that..."Uhm..my deck always loses to
>malkavian sneak bleed decks...but...uh...since my prey has a
>ravnos...and...I think that maybe he's got a sneak bleed deck...even
>though he did lie and bleed me out last game...uhm..I feal that for
>victory points in this game I should kill him..yeah thats it."

If there is strong evidence that you're using an out-of-game motivation,
yes, you do need to explain it.

Strong evidence (that would convince me, anyway) includes:

-The victimized player offended you in some way in a previous game (reneging
a deal, not taking an offered deal, whatever) AND the action you're taking
against him/her does not measurably improve your game position in any way
you can convincingly describe. (Spite)

-The action you're taking does not measurably improve your game position in
any way you can convincingly describe AND you don't have a pattern of random
behavior. (Collusion)

-You consistently fail to advance your own position, or even damage it, in
order to damage or attempt to damage a specific player's position. (Spite)

-You've exhibited a pattern of acting detrimental to your best interests
in blatant and obvious fashion over several turns/games (Collusion)

That last one's pretty squishy, and it'd have to be pretty darn blatant
before you graduated from 'just a dumbass' to 'probably throwing the game
in a partner's favor'.

>Is it judges or other players that will 'decide' what is collusion and
>what I can and can't do with my own deck?

Judges and other players already decide what you can and can't do with your
own deck. You can't, for example, put an Immortal Grapple back into your
hand from your ash heap for no reason, because the other players, and if
necessary judges, will bar you from doing so. This is just the same.

>Or is this just a rule made
>up to pick on certain players that noone likes, or that admit to using
>pre-determined tactics to cheat? (cause it seems totally pointless)

It may seem pointless, but it does address the issue of playing the
tournament rules instead of the game, which has been a problem for some
time.

>[no offense is intented (sic) at any person or group, I don't read all the

>posts, I just don't understand what this is supposed to accomplish,

>and how it will effect (sic) me]

It's supposed to keep you from avenging a betrayal in one round in the
next round. It's also supposed to keep you from cross-table (rushing, ousting,
whatever) a strong player just because you want to keep him/her from the
finals. With good judging, it'll accomplish that.

If you play each game in a tournament as a separate game, as you're supposed
to, the rule won't affect you at all, because you'll already be in compliance.

As the game becomes more and more popular, it will attract more and
more of the "bad" gamer, who cares about nothing and nobody but
himself and is perfectly willing to lie, cheat, steal, and do whatever
is necessary to get what he wants - including collude with another
person to gain the prize and then split it, no matter how
insignificant the prize.

Certain types of decks lend themselves well to disrupting the table...
Rush decks, random-vote decks, and the like. In the hands of a
malicious player, they can assuredly trash others' fun.

Keep in mind, however, that if a table keeps calling a judge over for
no reason, that the rest of the table (or person constantly calling
the judge) is likely to get a warning or two themselves on the order
of "please quit wasting my time."

Anyway, this discussion is bogging down in specific scenarios. I believe this
particular thread was started with someone wanting a simple answer. I further
believe that the point he was trying to make is that there is no such thing
because the interpretation of the rule is subjective. I don't see smooth
tournaments where someone spends 15 minutes explaining to the judge that it is,
in fact, in one's best interest to do something that looks stupid now because
the player anticipates the game to progress in some way that would otherwise be
at the player's disadvantage. What does the judge do when the judge doesn't
agree with the player's interpretation of how the game is likely to progress?

What is trying to be solved? Cheating? Only bad cheaters get caught. Bad
cheaters tend to also be bad players. Stupid players? Well, who knows how
stupid something is when players attempt to look ahead? Should Gomi have
gotten a penalty for Kindred Restructuring to become my prey as that ousted
him? I think so as that not only hurt him but potentially other players at the
table as well. But, what good does it do to penalize him after the fact?

Problem is that this rule is unenforceable in an even handed manner. Judges do
not know how a game is or will be going as well as a player playing in the
game. Competent rules breakers will likely be able to produce cause as to why
they are doing something against the spirt of the game. Etc.

All of this attempt to try and fix tournament play is nice in theory, but it is
superficial. Penalties, themselves, tend to be a less effective means of
producing good behavior. Instead, the incentives should be such that good
behavior is rewarded or, at least, not penalized. One of the ways to do this
is to make the rewards for winning tournaments relatively minor. For instance,
spread the prizes out across the tournament. That encourages players to show
up in the first place. The primary reward could be the satisfaction of winning
rather than gobbling up all the cool stuff.

With all the debates on this subject that we have seen here, I'm starting to
think that 'Laissez Faire' judging may be the way to go.

It is not always obvious what a Methuselah will gain by taking actions that
seem illogical, but that does not mean there is not a logical reason. Having
that Methuselah justify his/her intentions by explaining to a judge and
wasting time when frankly... the proof will be in the pudding.

Good players will win. Spiteful/Bad/Whatever players will most likely lose
and get a bad reputation for themselves.

Most of the time this will be the case... but if not, what can you
realistically do about it?

As someone who intends to try his hand at being a judge at an upcoming
tournament, I'd like to think that I'd allow cross-table nonsense,
regardless of its strategic value because I've seen too many games where
nonsense in turn five ends up as a win in turn six. Who am I to judge?
(Well... in this case, I *am* the judge heh).

It is very possible that some players will spitefully attack a player who
pissed them off or even collude together. However, I don't see how it is
possible to regulate this without delving into territory in which the judge
will be forced to make judgement calls based on knowing the intricacies of
not just that game, but the games and tourneys that preceded it plus any
player-player relationships that they are aware of that might influence the
game.

I went to Toronto with three other Detroit people and won the tournament.
Could it not be alleged that I convinced them to lose so that I would make
the finals? Such an accusation would not be unreasonable given the results
(though I assure you this was not the case--the other Detroiters simply
sucked ass--Hi Aaron!). How can I defend myself? How does a player address
this if they feel this is the case? It seems an awfully messy area we are
getting into frankly... and I think Aaron is right in questioning it.

Is it reasonable to think that maybe it would be better to have *less*
regulation along these lines? Instead of the rules as they currently are,
instead say 'Do whatever you want or need to win as long as you follow the
rules'? Collusion will still be looked down upon, as will spite. In fact, I
suspect that having the *respect* of your peers is a *lot* more important in
winning a tournament than the winning itself. If I win because I am a lying,
cheating, spiteful bastard... well, Yay. Who's gonna play with me? These
things regulate themselves somewhat.

Also, maybe in the same way that lying and deal-breaking is encouraged
within a given game, maybe a certain amount of out-of-game antics should
also be encouraged in the tournament as an event? Bear with me... if I
convinced the players that Aaron was a serious threat to make it to the
finals and they all attacked him incessantly through the first three
games... while I somehow made it to the finals because the focus was taken
off me, all we really have is the typical dynamic of one game reflected in
the tournament as a whole. As long as this is good-natured and everyone
agrees that it is 'part of the game' who loses really? (Well... Aaron loses,
but as I mentioned, he sucks ass).

This might result in a lot *less* deals than you'd think because everyone
would be so convinced that everyone else was manipulating them that they'd
probably just stick to concentrating on their own situation. Players who win
a match will be ever-so-humble in the next one because they *fear* the very
backlash/spite that we have just made legal. Essentially, it would just take
the 'Diplomacy' model a bit further... I've seen a lot of backstabbing and
betrayal that ends up being a big laugh after the game is over and I suspect
if this was extended to contain the entire tournament, the amount of
handshaking/drinking afterwards would be no less sincere.

Maybe I'm speaking out of my ass here... it's obvious the Detroit/Toronto
scene is markedly different from the way other groups play and frankly, as
things stand I have no problem with the VEKN rules. I predict certain
problems will arise, but I respect the intention of those that wrote them.

Cheers,
WES

In our experience playing locally, we have found that it is difficult
enough to break down your prey's defenses WHILE defending against your
predator, without wasting actions going cross-table randomly. We've
seen very small advantages turn into table sweeps. We've seen that
people with no pressure from their predator tend to do very well.
We've seen that people's decks generally run on a very fine balance,
and if you tip that balance over with cross-table actions, the entire
table tends to swing that way and collapse in someone's favor.

It is no accident that our games tend to last only 12 turns or so - we
are a vicious bunch here. We make no "table split" deals -- we're all
damned greedy and want all 4/5 VPs.

From this, I can conclude that when the game is played at a high
level, random cross-table actions are actually highly detrimental to
your OWN position - you waste an action, and you end up helping out
either your predator, prey, or both. If I kill my grandpredator's
first vampire (5 player table), then I cause myself two main problems:

My predator will have no pressure behind him, and will be all over me.
I will have to defend a lot more. If he is a fast deck, I may die on
the spot.

My grandprey will have no obstacle to gaining his own VPs, and can
rush forward rapidly. If he is a fast deck, I may have just handed
him one VP.

Since my own forward progress is slowed by having to defend against my
predator more, my likely best-case scenario is that by the time I oust
my prey by the skin of my teeth, my grandprey will have ousted both my
grandpredator and predator and is an excellent position. This leaves
me on the wrong end of a 2-1 split, and unless I happen to have a good
"stopper" deck for my final opponent, the table is likely to fall 4-1.

This leads me to believe that in general, destabilizing the table is
NOT a good thing to do unless you can be certain of the results.
Early on, you cannot be certain of the results, so destabilizing the
table is just a dumb idea. This is why Anarch Revolt decks are so
risky to play. If you drop 5 Anarch Revolts by turn 3, the table is
completely destabilized in favor of whoever is playing the fast bleed
deck. Since you don't know where the fast bleed deck is going to be

Everyone else also notices, because the Owl Companion mandates that
you show your hand to all players. Pesky card text.

>votes up on the table, and a prey with 1 pool. On his turn he chooses
>to do nothing. Can I call him for cheating, as it is obvious that the
>vote will succeed, gaining himself a VP?

No, although you've given a sadly incomplete picture of the situation,
so this cannot be a firm, 100% no. However...

There are many good reasons why he would wish to delay action.

- He may be worried about being intercepted and losing a vampire.

- He may wish to let his prey do more damage to his grandprey before
snagging the oust, speeding his process of gaining 2 VPs.

- He may want to solidify his position in some manner before moving
within intercept-range of his new prey - possibly by getting an extra
vampire out, possibly by cycling to some combat defense, possibly by
blocking you a few times and making you a weaker predator, possibly by
playing Disputed Territory and stealing an intercept location that
would be used against him later.

- In a rare subset of cases, he might actually want to let his prey
oust his grandprey FOR him... such as if the seating were Ventrue
vote, Gangrel unblockable bleed, and Tzimisce intercept. If he ousted
his Gangrel prey immediately, he could count on getting absolutely no
votes off and would die with 1VP. But the unblockable bleed should be
able to oust the Tzimisce, and then the Ventrue can run over the
Gangrel and move on with a better chance of gaining more than just the
1VP he was sure to gain anyway.

To determine any of the above for sure, additional information about
the game state is necessary.

>Can the 5.2 be used to compel action(or issue a warning) if someone is
>not killing their prey when it is obvious that they could?(as it can
>be used if someone is killing you cross table when they should be
>killing their prey)

It should never be used to compel an action, or to forbid an action.
It should only be used to issue cautions/warnings, etc.

Warnings might be issued if the circumstances were appropriate; for
example, if the player above REPEATEDLY declined to make any move
towards ousting his prey, I would start to be suspicious of
collusion... especially if his prey were close to ousting someone
himself. But delaying an oust for a turn or two is frequently a very
good strategic move, and in the situation I outlined above I wouldn't
even need an explanation -- it's obvious that the Ventrue need the
intercept deck gone to gain more than 1VP, and they need help doing
it.
